title: The ETF Review: The Value Fund Secretly Powered by Silicon Valley
subtitle: SEI's quant machine beats the benchmarks by slipping Big Tech into a bargain wrapper.
summary: SEI QiM U.S. Large Cap Value Active ETF strips down traditional multiples while loading up on artificial intelligence winners. It delivers market-beating returns, but anyone buying it for classic value safety is holding the same megacaps driving the broader rally.

bodyHtml:
You think you bought a dusty vault of rust-belt manufacturers, regional lenders, and beat-up utilities. You bought an artificial intelligence momentum portfolio wearing a tweed jacket.

Walk into the value aisle of the ETF supermarket and the pitch is familiar. You want protection from high-flying tech multiples. You want steady cash flows, low price-to-earnings ratios, and companies that pay you to wait. You spot the ticker SEIV, look at its dirt-cheap headline valuation, and assume you just bought an antidote to tech-heavy index concentration.

Look under the hood and the reality hits immediately. The fund’s largest single holding is Nvidia. Its third-largest position is Alphabet. Apple, Micron Technology, and Microsoft sit right alongside them near the top of the roster. A full third of the portfolio sits in technology.

SEIV is like a health-food diner where the chef secretly sautées everything in butter. The meal tastes incredible, the reviews are glowing, and the calorie count on the menu seems miraculously low. Yet the moment you ask why the food tastes so rich, the kitchen has to admit it is leaning heavily on the exact ingredients you came in to avoid.

Until June 2026, the fund called itself the SEI Enhanced U.S. Large Cap Value Factor ETF. The board quietly met, stripped out the academic "Enhanced Factor" label, and renamed it the SEI QiM U.S. Large Cap Value Active ETF.

The ticker stayed the same. The strategy did not budge an inch. Every major screening site still displays the old moniker, obscuring a simple reality: this is an aggressive, quant-driven active vehicle that buys the AI trade while printing a value multiple.

What You Actually Own

When you buy a standard large-cap index fund, cap-weighting does the driving. In a traditional cap-weighted fund, a company's footprint matches its total market value. If a tech titan triples in size, the fund automatically buys more, letting winners balloon while shrinking the laggards.

SEIV breaks that link completely. It holds just 123 names, compared to the 1,017 companies floating inside the Russell 1000. It concentrates its bets, yet keeps its risk distributed across the top. The top ten holdings account for 25.91% of total assets, and the largest single holding, Nvidia, commands just 3.94%. Apple follows at 3.49%, Alphabet at 2.50%, and Micron at 2.50%.

That top-ten roster is a strange hybrid of AI darlings and classic turnaround plays. Cardinal Health sits at 2.40%, General Motors at 2.38%, and Microsoft at 2.33%. Verizon, Citigroup, and Prudential Financial round out the leaders, each claiming just over 2% of the book.

Dig past the headline names and the portfolio gets grittier. Ranks eleven through twenty-five read like a bargain bin: HP Inc, CVS Health, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, AT&T, and Ford. You find beaten-down regional power names like Exelon and Edison International alongside post-restructuring plays like Expand Energy and United Airlines.

The sector allocations reveal the real active game. Technology is the heavyweight champion here at 32.69% of the fund. Financials come in second at 17.65%, followed by Health Care at 11.87% and Communication Services at 10.65%.

Compare those figures to its reporting benchmark, the Russell 1000, and the active tilts become obvious. The quant managers are running overweight bets on Financials by five percentage points and Utilities by three. They give extra room to Health Care and Communications while underweighting Industrials by five points and trimming broader tech exposure by four.

The size profile separates it even further from the index. Mega-cap giants with valuations north of $400 billion represent 48% of the Russell 1000, but they make up just 15% of SEIV. Instead, the fund dumps 35% of its capital into mid-cap names valued between $9 billion and $30 billion, compared to just 9% for the benchmark. The weighted average market capitalization of this portfolio sits near $613 billion, less than half the benchmark's $1.47 trillion footprint.

The immediate consequence of this layout is twofold. On one hand, no single company can blow up your capital; an absolute wipeout in its largest holding barely dings the NAV by four percent. On the other hand, five of the fund’s top seven holdings belong to the exact same AI infrastructure basket that dominates the rest of your portfolio.

Watch the holdings file at the end of each quarter to see if the technology weighting drifts closer to 40% or rotates toward beat-up cyclicals.

How the Sausage Is Made

SEIV is not an index fund. It does not track the Russell 1000; it merely uses that benchmark as a ruler to measure its results. There is no public index rulebook, no fixed calendar date when a third-party committee tells the fund what to buy, and no transparent single-stock caps.

Instead, the machine is managed by SEI’s Quantitative Investment Management team, known inside the firm as QiM. Operating out of London and Oaks, Pennsylvania, a team of six portfolio managers runs the show. Eugene Barbaneagra, Jianan Chen, Dante D’Orazio, Qi Shang, George Tyrakis, and Tianyu Xu share joint responsibility for the models.

The team feeds the large-cap universe into a two-step quantitative funnel. First comes the value filter. The model evaluates companies on earnings, cash flow, sales, and asset-based valuation characteristics. But instead of simply buying the cheapest hundred stocks on the board—which usually lands an investor in a graveyard of dying businesses—the engine runs an optimization step.

That optimizer blends the cheap valuations with secondary factors: momentum, quality, and low volatility. In practice, the computer searches for companies trading at reasonable multiples that are simultaneously showing improving earnings quality and positive share-price trends.

That multi-factor optimizer explains why names like Nvidia and Apple live inside a value portfolio. If a company's cash generation surges fast enough to bring down its relative multiples while its price trend stays vertical, the model sees a green light. Weightings do not mirror market caps. They mirror the optimizer’s conviction score.

That active tuning creates significant internal motion. The fund's prospectus puts the portfolio turnover rate at 44% of average portfolio value in its most recent fiscal year.

Yet SEIV operates inside a standard ETF wrapper, which gives it a structural advantage over old-fashioned mutual funds. Traditional funds must sell stock and raise cash whenever an investor leaves, triggering taxable capital gains distributions for everyone left behind.

An ETF avoids this through the creation and redemption process. When big institutions—known as Authorized Participants—need to create or redeem blocks of shares, they swap baskets of stock directly with the fund in-kind. Appreciated shares leave the fund tax-free, wiping away embedded capital gains before they can land on your year-end tax statement.

The mechanics run smoothly, but active quant churn means the fund is never on autopilot. Watch the trailing annual turnover metric in the next shareholder report to see whether portfolio churn stays near 44% or accelerates.

The Bill

The price tag on SEIV looks remarkably competitive at first glance. The fund charges an expense ratio of 0.15% per year. That is a unitary management fee: SEI pays all operating expenses out of that slice, leaving gross and net expenses identical with no marketing fees skimmed off the top.

Put that fee into real dollars over a decade. If you park $10,000 into SEIV, the fee eats $15 in year one, $48 after three years, and roughly $192 across a ten-year stretch. Its closest active structural rival, the Avantis U.S. Large Cap Value ETF (AVLV), charges the exact same 0.15%. Massive passive funds like the Vanguard Value ETF (VTV) cost less at 0.03%, but for an active quant strategy, fifteen basis points is practically wholesale pricing.

The hidden bills appear once you leave the prospectus and start trading. The median 30-day bid/ask spread on SEIV runs at 0.0788%, or roughly eight basis points. On a single round-trip trade, that spread is about eight times wider than the friction on broad market index trackers like SPY or VOO. If you move $50,000 into SEIV and bail six months later, you give up real money simply crossing the bid-ask line.

Liquidity tells a similar story. The fund trades roughly 125,000 shares on an average day, which translates to about $6.2 million in daily dollar volume. That is more than enough room for retail brokerage accounts, but institutional desks cannot sprint through the exit doors without moving the tape.

Then there is the tracking reality. Because SEIV does not follow an index, traditional tracking difference does not apply. Instead, look at tracking error, which measures how wildly an active manager deviates from the benchmark. SEIV runs a three-year tracking error of 6.13% against the Russell 1000. You are paying for a manager who wanders far from the reservation.

The pricing mechanism itself holds up well. Across hundreds of trading days, the fund traded at an average premium to net asset value of just 0.03%, never straying beyond a modest band. Authorized participants keep the market price glued tightly to the underlying assets.

Taxes, however, present a real drag despite the ETF wrapper. That 44% portfolio turnover means the fund trades rapidly through names. The prospectus after-tax numbers show that over a single year, a 27.26% pre-tax gain dropped to 16.42% once taxes on distributions and share sales were tallied. In an IRA or 401(k), that drag disappears. In a taxable brokerage account, it takes a heavy bite out of compounding.

Watch the average bid-ask spread during times of market volatility; if that eight-basis-point spread widens toward twenty, execution costs will devour your annual savings on the fee.

The Scoreboard

For all the quirky engineering, SEIV has delivered pure performance. Through the period ending September 30, 2026, the fund put up a 1-year total return of 28.18% on a net asset value basis. Its three-year annualized return landed at 26.85%. Since its launch in May 2022, it has generated an annualized return of 18.94%, producing a cumulative gain of 113.46%.

The benchmark looks pedestrian beside it. Over the same three-year stretch, the Russell 1000 posted an annualized return of 22.48%, while the S&P 500 managed 22.89%. Over the trailing twelve months, SEIV outran its Russell benchmark by more than 13 percentage points.

Stack it against rivals through mid-October 2026, and SEIV retains its lead over the passive establishment. Its year-to-date return of 20.81% and trailing one-year mark of 31.72% easily beat traditional passive giants. The Vanguard Value ETF gained 21.77% over the past year, while the iShares Russell 1000 Value ETF (IWD) returned 27.68%. Pure-value index options lagged even further: the Invesco S&P 500 Pure Value ETF (RPV) climbed 24.35%, and the Schwab U.S. Large-Cap Value ETF (SCHV) posted 19.88%.

Its only true peer, Avantis's active AVLV, ran neck-and-neck, delivering a 31.14% one-year gain. The only fund that left SEIV in the dust was the iShares MSCI USA Value Factor ETF (VLUE), which surged nearly 60% over the year. Yet that gap was not a triumph of pure value investing; it was an artifact of VLUE’s massive, concentrated allocation to soaring semiconductor stocks.

The most compelling feature on SEIV’s scoreboard is how cheap it looks while posting those numbers. The fund sports a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of 13.67. The S&P 500 trades at 25.16. That means SEIV is priced at roughly 54% of the broader market’s multiple.

On a forward-looking basis, the gap widens. The fund carries a median forward P/E of 11.14 against 20.25 for the Russell 1000. Its price-to-book ratio sits at 2.30, less than half the index level of 5.40. It also offers a modest yield cushion, with a dividend yield of 1.58% compared to less than 1% on broad market trackers.

Risk metrics reflect the active buffering. The fund posts a beta of 0.69, suggesting it moves substantially less than the wider market on down days. Its three-year annualized standard deviation sits at 12.64%, a hair below the Russell 1000’s 13.07%.

Watch the performance gap between SEIV and AVLV over the coming quarters to see whether SEI’s quant optimizer can maintain its edge against its primary active competitor.

What You're Really Betting On

When you buy SEIV, you are not betting on the classic value playbook. You are betting that a quantitative computer can strip-mine the stock market for cheap cash flows, graft a momentum engine onto the back, and steer clear of classic value traps.

You are betting that valuation metrics alone are useless without trend confirmation. In plain terms: you are wagering that cheap stocks only work when the market is actively starting to notice them.

Now listen to the short seller's argument, because the bear case against this fund cuts straight to the bone.

Strip away the marketing labels and SEIV is a tech-heavy momentum vehicle masquerading as a defensive value hedge. The fund's own annual shareholder report for fiscal 2026 gave the game away in black ink: value factors delivered flat performance across the entire large-cap universe over the period. The fund beat its benchmark solely because secondary momentum positioning carried the load, while quality factors were an outright drag. The report explicitly noted that an underweight position in Nvidia actually hurt performance.

Five of the fund's top seven holdings are the exact same megacap tech giants driving the rest of the market. Buying this fund to diversify away from index concentration is an illusion.

Worse, that rock-bottom trailing P/E of 13.67 is an engineered mirage. The multiple looks incredibly cheap because it is heavily weighed down by cyclically peaking profits in auto manufacturing, semiconductors, and memory hardware: Micron, General Motors, Ford, and HP. When cyclical earnings reach their peak, stocks always look their cheapest right before profits collapse. That is the definition of a value trap.

A beta of 0.69 will not protect you if the AI capital expenditure cycle rolls over. If hyperscalers slash their chip spending, the cyclically inflated earnings supporting these tech names will evaporate, pulling down both the headline multiples and the share prices at the exact same time.

What proves the bears right? Watch what happens during a sustained period where pure value stocks lead the market while tech momentum stalls out. If the AI complex suffers an earnings correction while boring industrials rally, SEIV's tech-heavy book will drag it straight to the bottom of the value category.

How to Use It

SEIV does not work as a standalone core holding for your entire portfolio. It is far too idiosyncratic, carries too much tracking error, and wanders too far from broader market exposure to replace a simple total market allocation.

Instead, this fund functions as an aggressive satellite position or a direct replacement for stale large-cap value funds. If you hold an aging allocation to a passive tracker like VTV, IWD, or SCHV, swapping into SEIV hands you active factor optimization for roughly twelve basis points more. You trade away cap-weighted passivity in exchange for momentum-driven upside.

It suits the modern investor who wants exposure to lower-multiple equities without being dragged down by traditional value "zombies"—companies that are cheap for good reason and never recover. It fits an investor comfortable with factor volatility who wants an active edge at a rock-bottom fifteen-basis-point price tag.

It completely fails the investor who wants a true, safe-haven value shelter. If your goal is to hedge against a massive correction in Big Tech and AI infrastructure, owning SEIV is counterproductive. You are simply re-buying the same silicon trade through an alternate door. It is also the wrong tool for high-frequency traders who will get clipped by the eight-basis-point spread, or for high earners building positions in taxable accounts who cannot afford annual capital gains friction.

The Verdict

SEI QiM U.S. Large Cap Value Active ETF gives investors a brilliantly engineered, low-cost factor machine that consistently beats its benchmark, but it achieves those results by smuggling Silicon Valley into the value aisle.

Watch the portfolio's technology sector weighting at the next semi-annual disclosure to see if SEI trims its AI exposure when momentum finally cools.

Analysis, not advice. We may own these names and we may sell them at any time.
